REDLINE REVIEW MEMORANDUM
Funds Asset Management — Investment Advisory Agreement

PRIVILEGED & CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT

TO:      Engagement File — Funds Asset Management (Matter File 15)
FROM:    [Associate], Corporate & Funds Group
RE:      Redline Review of Counterparty Markup of Investment Advisory Agreement Against Standard Form and Internal Playbook
DATE:    [Current Date]

I. PURPOSE AND SCOPE

This memorandum documents our comprehensive redline review of the counterparty's markup of the Investment Advisory Agreement (the "Agreement") against the firm's standard form and the internal funds-asset-management playbook. This review reconciles every deviation introduced in the counterparty markup, assesses each against the firm's baseline negotiating position and the applicable regulatory framework governing investment advisers (including the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, as amended), and recommends an accept / reject / counter position for each item.

For purposes of this review, the operative deal materials are the matter file for the funds-asset-management engagement. Consistent with the engagement instruction, this review addresses each provision flagged by counsel for analysis against firm precedent and market practice. Any correspondence in the matter folder from an unrelated engagement has been disregarded as misfiled and does not inform this analysis.

II. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

The counterparty markup, taken as a whole, shifts material risk to the adviser in several respects and, if accepted without modification, would (i) broaden the adviser's indemnification exposure beyond market norms, (ii) weaken the adviser's ability to terminate the relationship on an orderly basis, (iii) expand the scope and duration of representations and warranties, and (iv) narrow the conditions to closing in a manner favorable only to the client. We recommend a firm counterposition on the high-priority items below, and acceptance of the counterparty's more benign conforming edits.

Summary of recommended positions:

- Indemnification scope: REJECT the expansion; COUNTER with adviser-side standard carve-outs.
- Termination rights: REJECT the elimination of the adviser's convenience/for-cause termination basket; COUNTER with a qualified termination right.
- Representations and warranties survival: REJECT extension of survival beyond the standard period; COUNTER with the firm's standard survival term.
- Amendment/waiver: REJECT the unilateral auto-renewal and oral-waiver provisions.
- Conditions to closing: ACCEPT the closing-condition clean-up edits, subject to the adviser's customary "no material adverse change" qualifier.

III. AGREEMENT STRUCTURE AND PARTIES

The Agreement governs the provision of discretionary and non-discretionary investment advisory services by the adviser to the client fund and its feeder vehicles. Material structural points:

- Services include portfolio management, trade execution, and on-going compliance and reporting support.
- Compensation is an asset-based management fee, calculated quarterly on average daily AUM, plus performance allocation as separately agreed.
- The Agreement contemplates automatic renewal with a right of non-renewal upon notice, and termination for cause or upon the adviser's resignation.

Against this backdrop, the counterparty's markup edits in the sections below require particular attention.

IV. REPRESENTATIONS AND WARRANTIES

A. Adviser Representations — Standard Form Baseline
The standard form includes customary adviser representations limited to: valid existence and authority; registration status as an investment adviser with the SEC; authority to execute and perform; the absence of conflict under material agreements; and accuracy of the adviser's Form ADV disclosures.

B. Counterparty Markup Deviations
1. Expanded "no default" representation. The counterparty markup adds a representation that the adviser is not in default under "any material agreement," without a "reasonably expects" or "knowledge" qualifier and without a materiality carve-out. This is broader than standard market practice and could be breached inadvertently by ministerial defaults unrelated to the engagement.
— Recommendation: REJECT / COUNTER to "no material default under any material agreement that would reasonably be expected to have a Material Adverse Effect on the performance of the adviser's obligations hereunder."

2. Survival extension. The counterparty extends the survival of the adviser's representations and warranties from the standard 24-month post-termination period to indefinitely. This exceeds market norm and the playbook ceiling.
— Recommendation: REJECT / COUNTER to firm-standard survival (24 months from termination or the date fees are finally determined, whichever is earlier).

3. Client/any-party representations. The counterparty has added representations for the client as to the accuracy of information provided, but has done so asymmetrically, omitting the standard "as of the date of the reliance" qualifier. This is largely conforming but should be tightened.
— Recommendation: ACCEPT with conforming modification to add "as of the Effective Date and on the date any related reliance statement is delivered."

C. Playbook Considerations
The internal playbook identifies adviser representations as a core protective category. The counterparty's markup increases the adviser's exposure without corresponding consideration. Recommend holding firm on the standard scope of adviser reps.

V. COVENANTS

A. Standard Form Baseline
The standard form contains limited operational covenants: compliance with applicable law and the adviser's fiduciary duties; maintenance of registration and books and records; notification of material changes to Form ADV; and compliance with the client fund's governing documents and regulatory directives.

B. Counterparty Markup Deviations
1. New affirmative covenant — information systems and cybersecurity. The counterparty adds a broad covenant requiring the adviser to maintain cybersecurity and business continuity programs "in accordance with the highest industry standards," without a reasonableness standard. Given regulatory guidance on adviser cybersecurity (SEC RIN 3235-AM64), a defined and reasonable standard is advisable.
— Recommendation: COUNTER to maintain "reasonable cybersecurity and business-continuity safeguards commensurate with industry practice for investment advisers of comparable size and scope."

2. Affirmative covenant — new asset-class/strategy restriction. The counterparty introduces a covenant requiring the adviser to obtain prior written approval before investing in "new asset classes." This unreasonably constrains discretionary authority and is inconsistent with the fund's stated strategy.
— Recommendation: REJECT / COUNTER to require advance notice (not approval) for asset classes outside the strategy set forth in the fund's offering documents.

3. Negative covenant — restrictions on soft dollars / directed brokerage. The counterparty adds a covenant restricting the adviser's use of soft dollars and directed brokerage, which conflicts with the adviser's discretionary authority over execution and the fund's approved brokerage arrangements.
— Recommendation: REJECT to the extent it conflicts with the fund's approved brokerage/proxy arrangements; COUNTER to conform to the fund's governing documents.

C. Playbook Considerations
The playbook prescribes that operational covenants should be tied to a "reasonable standards" metric and should not intrude on the adviser's discretionary investment authority. Deviations expanding affirmative covenants beyond that framework should be rejected.

VI. CONDITIONS TO CLOSING

A. Standard Form Baseline
Conditions to the adviser's obligation to commence services are limited to: receipt of a signed agreement; delivery of the executed fund documents; and the client's agreement to the fee and allocation terms.

B. Counterparty Markup Deviations
1. New condition — execution of a separate custody agreement and IRA. The counterparty adds conditions requiring execution of a separate custody agreement and investment management agreement prior to closing. These are reasonable conforming requirements.
— Recommendation: ACCEPT, subject to the adviser's customary "no material adverse change in the client's regulatory or financial condition" qualifier.

2. Broadened "accuracy of representations" condition. The counterparty rewords the closing condition to require all adviser representations to be true "in all respects," rather than "in all material respects, except where the representation is qualified by materiality."
— Recommendation: COUNTER to restore the "in all material respects" standard.

C. Playbook Considerations
The playbook requires that closing conditions for the adviser be limited in number and scope. The markup's additions are largely acceptable as conforming; the "in all respects" reword is not.

VII. INDEMNIFICATION

A. Standard Form Baseline
The standard form provides: (i) the client indemnifies the adviser for losses arising out of the adviser's good-faith provision of services, the client's instructions, and investment decisions made in accordance with the fund strategy; and (ii) the adviser indemnifies the client only for the adviser's gross negligence, willful misconduct, fraud, or material breach of the agreement.

B. Counterparty Markup Deviations
1. Standard reduction — adviser indemnification on ordinary negligence. The counterparty rewrites the adviser's indemnity to cover "any negligent act or omission" (ordinary negligence), deleting the "gross negligence or willful misconduct" standard. This is the single most significant adverse deviation.
— Recommendation: REJECT / COUNTER firmly to the firm-standard "gross negligence, willful misconduct, bad faith, or material breach" standard.

2. Expansion of client-side indemnity carve-outs. The counterparty narrows the client's indemnity of the adviser by adding carve-outs for losses arising from the adviser's "failure to comply with any applicable law." Unqualified, this could strip the client indemnity in most scenarios.
— Recommendation: COUNTER to carve out only "grossly negligent or intentional violation of applicable law by the adviser."

3. New cap and subrogation provisions. The counterparty adds a liability cap of 12 months' fees and a subrogation clause directing any insurer subrogation recovery to the client. A cap is market-acceptable in the funds context but should be set at the playbook reference (24 months' fees) and should not apply to fiduciary-breach or fraud claims.
— Recommendation: COUNTER on the cap amount and carve out fraud/willful misconduct.

C. Playbook Considerations
Indemnification is a high-priority protective provision. The playbook directs that the adviser's indemnity be limited to gross negligence/willful misconduct, and that any cap exclude fraud. The counterparty's ordinary-negligence shift must be rejected.

VIII. TERMINATION

A. Standard Form Baseline
The Agreement permits termination for cause, upon notice for non-renewal, and by the adviser for a change of control at the client or for non-payment of fees. Fees earned through termination are payable, and there is a standard transition assistance provision.

B. Counterparty Markup Deviations
1. Elimination of the adviser's termination for non-payment. The counterparty deletes the adviser's right to terminate for the client's non-payment of fees.
— Recommendation: REJECT / COUNTER to reinstate the adviser's termination right for unpaid fees after notice and a cure period.

2. Automatic renewal with shortened non-renewal notice. The counterparty reduces the non-renewal notice period from 60 days to 30 days and makes renewal automatic with no opt-out acknowledgment. This shortens the adviser's planning window.
— Recommendation: COUNTER to restore a 60-day non-renewal notice period.

3. Termination for cause — narrowed cause definition. The counterparty narrows "cause" to exclude the client's material breach of its own funding or information obligations.
— Recommendation: COUNTER to add the client's material breach of the agreement as a cause event relating to the adviser's termination rights.

4. Transition assistance fee. The counterparty seeks to convert the adviser's post-termination transition assistance into an uncompensated obligation. Under market practice and the playbook, transition assistance is compensated at the adviser's then-current rates or a negotiated transition fee.
— Recommendation: COUNTER to retain the firm-standard compensated transition provision.

C. Playbook Considerations
Termination provisions are a two-way street; the playbook instructs that the adviser must retain a for-cause and non-payment termination right, and a reasonable renewal/notice framework.

IX. FEE AND COMPENSATION PROVISIONS

A. Standard Form Baseline
The standard form sets a quarterly management fee calculated on period-average AUM, payable in arrears, with performance allocation as separately set forth, and a fee-dispute resolution procedure.

B. Counterparty Markup Deviations
1. Fee calculation change. The counterparty changes the fee base from "average daily AUM" to "AUM as of the last business day of the quarter," which penalizes the adviser on inflows during the quarter.
— Recommendation: COUNTER to retain the period-average daily AUM basis consistent with the playbook.

2. Late-fee waiver / interest. The counterparty deletes accrued interest on late fees and broadens the client's ability to withhold fees during disputed invoices.
— Recommendation: COUNTER to reinstate standard late-payment interest at the prime rate plus 2%, and to limit withholding to the disputed amount only.

X. AMENDMENT, WAIVER, AND GENERAL PROVISIONS

A. Amendment/Waiver. The counterparty removes the requirement that amendments be in writing and signed by both parties, replacing it with a unilateral modification right for "administrative changes." Oral amendments and unilateral modification are unacceptable and inconsistent with the standard form.
— Recommendation: REJECT / COUNTER to require any amendment or waiver to be in writing and executed by the authorized representatives of both parties.

B. Assignment. The counterparty adds a consent right allowing the client to assign without the adviser's consent upon a change of control. This is acceptable only if the assignee is financially and operationally able, and sensitive client information remains protected. Recommending a counter that the assignment be to an "institutional successor" with the adviser's consent not to be unreasonably withheld.

C. Confidentiality / Data Protection. The counterparty adds a broad data-protection annex expanding the adviser's obligations concerning client data, including a new requirement to provide "all records" upon request without cost. Recommending acceptance of reasonable data-protection obligations, but countering the "all records at no cost" provision to conform to the firm-standard records-retention and reasonable-cost framework (consistent with Advisers Act Rule 204-2 considerations).

D. Governing Law / Dispute Resolution. The counterparty changes the governing law from New York to the client's home jurisdiction and adds mandatory mediation before any legal proceeding. COUNTER to retain New York governing law and the firm-standard dispute-resolution provision, given the adviser's nationwide regulatory footprint, but accept a non-binding pre-suit good-faith negotiation period.

XI. DEVIATION LOG — SUMMARY RECOMMENDATIONS

Each deviation identified above is logged below with its recommended disposition:

1. Expanded No-Default Rep — REJECT / COUNTER (add materiality and reasonable-expectation qualifiers).
2. Indefinite Rep Survival — REJECT / COUNTER (24-month firm-standard survival).
3. Client Rep "As Of" Qualifier — ACCEPT with conforming edit.
4. Cybersecurity Covenant — COUNTER to "reasonable safeguards."
5. New-Asset-Class Prior Approval — REJECT / COUNTER to advance notice.
6. Soft-Dollar/Directed Brokerage Restriction — REJECT (conflicts with fund arrangements); COUNTER to conform to governing doc.
7. Closing Condition — Custody/IMA execution — ACCEPT with no-MAC qualifier.
8. Closing Condition — "In All Respects" standard — COUNTER to "in all material respects."
9. Adviser Indemnity on Ordinary Negligence — REJECT (high priority, hold firm).
10. Client Indemnity Carve-Out (law violation) — COUNTER to grossly negligent violation only.
11. Liability Cap 12 months & subrogation — COUNTER to 24 months and carve except fraud.
12. Termination for Non-Payment Deleted — REJECT / COUNTER to reinstate.
13. Non-Renewal Notice 30 days — COUNTER to 60 days.
14. Cause Definition Narrowed — COUNTER to add client material breach.
15. Transition Assistance Uncompensated — COUNTER to compensated transition.
16. Fee Basis Change — COUNTER to average-daily-AUM.
17. Late-Fee/Withholding Change — COUNTER to reinstate interest and narrow withholding.
18. Oral/Unilateral Amendment — REJECT (high priority).
19. Assignment Consent — COUNTER to institutional-successor standard.
20. Records-at-No-Cost — COUNTER to firm-standard records/retention framework.
21. Governing Law Change — COUNTER to retain New York law.

XII. NEGOTIATING PRIORITIES AND FALLBACKS

Priority 1 (must hold — deal-critical): Items 1, 9, 18 (indemnification standard, rep scope, written amendments). These are the contractual core and should not be conceded.
Priority 2 (strong preference — seek to hold but may compromise): Items 2, 12, 13, 15, 16, 21 (survival, termination, fees, governing law).
Priority 3 (acceptable to trade in exchange for Priority 1/2): Items 6, 7, 19, 20 (accommodating conforming items) where the counterparty demonstrates a genuine operational need.

Fallback positions: If the counterparty insists on an ordinary-negligence indemnity standard, counter for a liability cap substantially below the firm reference (e.g., 6 months' fees) and an explicit carve-out for gross negligence, willful misconduct, fraud, and breaches of fiduciary duty, plus a "first-dollar" structure that is uncapped for the excluded conduct.

XIII. REGULATORY FRAMEWORK CONSIDERATIONS

Any revisions must remain consistent with the adviser's obligations under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, including the fiduciary duties of care and loyalty, Rule 204-2 recordkeeping, Rule 206(4)-7 compliance-program requirements, and current SEC cybersecurity and ESG disclosure expectations. The recommended positions above are drafted to preserve these obligations while allocating ordinary business risk to the party best positioned to bear it.

XIV. CONCLUSION AND NEXT STEPS

The counterparty markup contains a number of conforming and acceptable edits, but it also introduces several material risk-shifting deviations that are inconsistent with the firm's standard form and the internal playbook. We recommend returning a redline that accepts the conforming items, counters on the priority-1 and priority-2 items as described above, and preserves the adviser's core protective provisions.

Next steps: (1) circulate this memo to the responsible partner for approval of the recommended positions; (2) prepare the counter-redline incorporating the recommendations; and (3) schedule a negotiation call to resolve the priority-1 items before finalizing the Agreement.

Please contact the undersigned with any questions.

[Associate]
Corporate & Funds Group
